title: How AI like ChatGPT works, explained
excerpt: How AI like ChatGPT works, explained in plain language with interactive diagrams: language models, agents and AI security. Updated every month.
content_html:
November 2026 edition

How AI like ChatGPT works, updated every month

Most of us use AI tools every day without knowing what happens between typing a question and getting an answer. This guide explains it from the ground up, in plain language, with diagrams you can try.

Here for security? Start with prompt injection (14 min, no earlier chapters needed).

One generation step, shown for three example prompts

Your text, as tokens

Each token then becomes a long list of numbers (24 of thousands shown):

Next-token probabilities

Real numbers from SmolLM2-360M, a small open model. It scores all 49,152 tokens in its vocabulary; these are the most likely.

Part 1: Language models

How a language model turns text into numbers, predicts the next word and learns from data, and where that breaks down. Each chapter has a demo to try and three questions at the end. New to this? Start with chapter 1; otherwise jump around.

1

What an LLM is, in five minutes

The whole picture in five minutes: what these systems are, how they were built and what they are not.

6 min

2

Text becomes tokens, tokens become numbers

Models never see letters or words. They see numbered pieces of text, and then points on a map of meaning.

10 min

3

Attention: how words borrow meaning

How each word looks back at the earlier words and pulls in what it needs. This is the core mechanism of the transformer.

10 min

4

Inside the stack

Each layer gathers context from other words and then processes it, and a model repeats that dozens of times. Also: the trick that lets giant models run cheaply.

9 min

5

Generating text, one token at a time

Each word is a weighted dice roll. That explains why answers differ every time, what "temperature" does and why thinking takes time.

12 min

6

Training: from autocomplete to assistant to agent

A model goes through five training stages, and each one changes what it does. Knowing them explains a lot of everyday behaviour.

11 min

7

Is it really just predicting the next word?

Technically, it is. Training, the model's internal representations and the tool loop explain why a coding agent can still do far more than autocomplete.

15 min

8

What they're good at, and where it breaks

Why these models are good at some things and reliably bad at others, including a security problem nobody has solved.

12 min

Mixed review · 5 questions that combine the chapters of this part

How we got here · optional, 6 minutes. Six turning points, from image recognition to agents, and the chapters that explain each one.

Part 2: Agents

Agents are language models that use tools and act on your behalf. These chapters cover the loop, what the model sees at each step, what agents get done in practice and how to tell when they fail.

1

From chat to agent: tools and the loop

An agent is a language model called again and again, with tools in between. Step through the loop and see why small mistakes add up and what each step costs.

12 min

2

What the agent sees: context, memory and plug-ins

The model only knows what the harness puts in front of it: how the context fills up, what product "memory" really is, how tools plug in, and where agent code should run.

13 min

3

Around the model: small models, decision models, harnesses

Most AI products combine several models with plain software. Who does what, and where the new decision models fit.

12 min

4

Agents at work: code, computers and long tasks

Agents do best where every step can be checked. What they handle today, how long a job you can hand over, and why benchmark results and real work disagree.

13 min

5

When agents fail, and how to tell

Agents often report success they didn't achieve. Why "the tests pass" and "I'm done" are weak evidence, what lab tests of deception show, and which kinds of oversight work.

13 min

Mixed review · 5 questions that combine the chapters of this part

Part 3: Trust & security

What goes wrong when AI reads, acts and remembers on your behalf, and the habits and controls that still help when a model is fooled. Written for everyday users and for the people who build and defend these systems.

1

When text becomes a command: prompt injection

Why a stranger's email can take over your assistant, why better wording won't fix it, and the designs that do.

14 min

2

Giving an AI the keys: agents and permissions

Least privilege, sandboxes and egress rules are the controls that still work when both the model and the human slip.

13 min

3

Poisoned ingredients: the AI supply chain

Invented package names, model files that run code, poisoned training data, and what signing can and can't promise.

12 min

4

Where your words go: your data and the model

Training, retention, human review, memory and share links, explained without the legalese, plus what EU law says.

12 min

5

Finding got cheap: AI and the patch gap

AI now finds software flaws faster than anyone can fix them. Why the hard part of security moved to patching, and what still works.

12 min

6

Don't trust the scoreboard: judging AI claims

How to read benchmarks, vendor security numbers, AI detectors and deepfakes, with habits for telling what's real.

15 min

Mixed review · 5 questions that combine the chapters of this part

Part 4: Looking ahead

Where research is trying to fix today's limits, and the guide's main points and habits on one page.

Final review · 6 questions that combine the chapters of this part

This month in the field
